# LAYER 4 — The report

Ground truth for synthesis and prose. Written against the live six-section template, within its word limits.

---

## A. Summary and Overview

The Girls Return to Learning and Safety Programme, FCDO programme code MWI-EDU-AR-4471, has completed its first year of implementation in Machinga and Mangochi districts, Malawi. FCDO approved £1,240,000 for the full period, which runs from 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2026, with an inception phase to 31 December 2024. BridgeLight Education Trust delivers the programme with district education offices, community-based organisations, parent-teacher associations and girls' clubs.

One qualification applies to everything that follows and should be read first. The award letter sets the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025. All indicator and financial data available for this review has been prepared on a 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025 basis, because that is the cycle partner reports were submitted on and the finance data has not been recut. Every figure in this report therefore describes a twelve-month window that opens and closes a fortnight earlier than the contractual one. No written amendment to the review period has been agreed. The difference is unlikely to change the direction of any finding, but it does mean nothing here can be presented as a precise statement of contractual-period performance.

Output delivery in year one was mixed. Of the twelve output indicators in the results framework, ten carry an achieved value. Five met or exceeded their Year 1 milestone: 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a milestone of 650; 438 girls completing at least twenty remedial learning sessions against 420; 31 lockable latrine stances rehabilitated or newly functional against 24; 571 girls receiving a re-entry kit or learning materials package against 550; and 136 school and community actors trained against 120. Five fell short: 472 supported girls attending at least 80 per cent of school days against a milestone of 500; 17 schools with menstrual health supplies and a trained focal teacher against 20; 392 caregivers receiving a hardship grant against 400; 68 per cent of hardship grant households with verified attendance follow-up within 45 days against 75 per cent; and three district learning meetings held against four.

Two indicators were not reported at all. There is no achieved value for schools with an active safeguarding referral pathway tested through a termly case-review meeting, or for learning briefs produced and shared with district stakeholders. Both carried Year 1 milestones. Their absence is a reporting gap rather than evidence of non-delivery, and it cannot be resolved from the material available for this review.

The most serious limitation is at outcome level. The programme's three outcome indicators cover attendance, progression and girls' own sense of safety at school and in travel. None has an achieved value for the year. The results export covers output performance only. The Annual Review is required to assess the Outcome, and on the evidence held that assessment cannot be made. Output-level attendance data exists, but it counts a different population on a different definition, and treating it as an outcome proxy would misstate performance to FCDO.

Expenditure attributed to indicators for the year was £920,420 against a forecast of £880,000, an overspend of £40,420 or 4.6 per cent. The largest single variance is in WASH rehabilitation, where cement and transport costs ran £27,900 above forecast, followed by Output 1 field costs, where lake-shore school locations drove transport higher. Three lines underspent, the largest being attendance follow-up, where an M&E assistant post stood vacant. A programme-level forecast against actual statement covering the full £1,240,000 award, which the award letter requires in the review pack, has not been prepared. The source data also acknowledges that cost attribution at indicator level is imperfect, with staff time recorded against attendance monitoring that may belong under Output 4.

The main issues for FCDO's attention are these. The outcome assessment cannot be completed on the evidence provided. Two output indicators are unreported. The reporting period does not match the contract and has not been formally varied. Disaggregated figures do not reconcile to headline totals in three places, and the caregiver breakdown is not credible on its face. The proposed output scores in the export are marked draft and were prepared at indicator level rather than output level, so they are not in a form FCDO can adopt at this review.

Four priorities follow, set out in full in the final section. BridgeLight should resolve the reporting period, either by recutting the data or by securing written agreement to the October to September cycle. It should report the two missing output indicators. It should put outcome-level measurement in place and report against it before the second Annual Review. And it should reconcile disaggregated data to headline figures before any further results are submitted.

## B. Performance and Conclusions

**Outcome performance.** The programme's outcome is that adolescent girls targeted by the programme demonstrate improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity by September 2026, with reduced practical and safeguarding barriers to education. Three indicators measure it: the share of supported girls attending school at least 80 per cent of days in the last completed term, baseline 38 per cent against a Year 1 milestone of 55; the share progressing to the next grade or completing a re-entry pathway, baseline 31 per cent against a milestone of 48; and the share reporting that school is safe during menstruation and travel, baseline 41 per cent against a milestone of 58.

No achieved value is available for any of the three. The results export prepared for this review contains output-level rows only. BridgeLight's monitoring design anticipates quarterly survey tools, which would be the natural source, but no survey results have been provided. **The Annual Review therefore cannot assess Outcome achievement for year one.** This is stated plainly rather than worked around: output data measuring related concepts exists, but it counts individuals reached rather than the proportion of a defined population, and substituting it would produce a figure that looks like an outcome result and is not one.

**Output performance against expected results.** Output 1, girls re-entering and remaining in education, weighted at 35 per cent, performed above expectation on two of three indicators. Re-enrolment and retention reached 684 against a milestone of 650, drawn from school registers, re-entry club forms and a district validation sample. Remedial learning completion reached 438 against 420. Sustained attendance was the shortfall, at 472 against a milestone of 500, attributed to late register submission from four of the forty schools in scope.

Output 2, safer WASH and safeguarding conditions, weighted at 25 per cent, was mixed. Latrine rehabilitation reached 31 stances against a milestone of 24, though four units still lack disposal bins and the indicator does not make clear whether the figure includes the six stances functional at baseline. Menstrual health provision fell short at 17 schools against 20, because three schools had no female focal teacher available. The third indicator, safeguarding referral pathways tested through case-review meetings, is unreported.

Output 3, reducing household cost barriers, weighted at 25 per cent and carrying the highest design risk rating, fell short on two of three indicators. Hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a milestone of 400, after sixteen duplicate caregiver records were removed. Re-entry kits exceeded expectation at 571 against 550. Verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 68 per cent against a milestone of 75, because September follow-ups were incomplete at the point of reporting.

Output 4, district evidence use, weighted at 15 per cent, delivered three of four planned learning meetings, one having been cancelled during the district examination period, and trained 136 school and community actors against a milestone of 120. Learning brief production is unreported.

**Major deviations.** Three deviations warrant FCDO's attention beyond individual indicator variance. The absence of outcome data is the most significant. The unreported OP2.3 indicator matters disproportionately because it is the programme's only measure of whether safeguarding systems are functioning in practice rather than on paper, in a programme FCDO rated Medium-High risk partly for safeguarding sensitivity. And the reported re-enrolment figure moved from 612 in a September internal note to 684 in the October export, described as the result of removing double-count risk. Deduplication reduces a count; it does not raise one by 72. The 684 is reported here as the verified figure because it comes from the later validated export, but the movement is unexplained.

**Disaggregation.** The award letter requires monitoring data to be disaggregated by gender, age and vulnerability group where relevant, and the results export carries columns for all three. The data is not currently reliable enough to support that requirement. For the two largest Output 1 indicators, the sex and age cells fall three and one short of the reported headline. For hardship grants, all 392 recipients are recorded as male and distributed across age bands of 6–11, 12–17 and 18–24, which cannot describe caregivers in a programme delivered substantially through mother groups. For district learning meetings, three meetings are disaggregated across person-level bands totalling 39, apparently describing attendees rather than the indicator itself. The vulnerability totals also do not reconcile: the previously married or early union column sums to 227 against a stated total of 291.

Where disaggregation does hold, it shows the expected pattern. Girls aged 12–17 make up the large majority of those re-enrolled, attending regularly, completing remedial sessions and receiving kits, with smaller numbers in the 6–11 and 18–24 bands. Ultra-poor households and girls with disabilities are represented across all four Output 1 and Output 3 indicators. It should be noted that the monitoring age bands do not align with the stated target population of girls aged 10–19, so a share of those counted sit outside the intended range at both ends.

One further clarification. The totals row of the results export sums each column across all indicators. Those totals are not beneficiary counts — the same girl appears under several indicators — and they should not be read as programme reach.

## Evidence and Evaluation

**Strength of the evidence base.** The evidence supporting output claims is administrative and, for the most part, appropriate to what is being measured. Re-enrolment rests on school registers and re-entry club forms with a district validation sample, which is the strongest evidence chain in the review. Attendance draws on term 3 registers from 36 of the 40 schools in scope. WASH claims are supported by engineer completion certificates and school verification photographs. Hardship grant delivery is evidenced by mobile money payment records with an attendance follow-up sample. Training and meeting claims rest on attendance sheets, with pre- and post-training quiz forms for the actor training indicator.

The pattern across these sources is consistent: BridgeLight can substantiate that activities took place and that individuals were reached. The award letter requires evidence for every numeric claim included in the review, and for the ten reported output indicators that requirement is met in principle, though none of the underlying records has been examined as part of this review.

**Where the evidence base is weak.** It is weak in exactly the place that matters most. There is no outcome-level evidence at all. The monitoring design names quarterly survey tools, which would generate the attendance, progression and safety perception data the outcome indicators require, but no survey output has been provided and it is not clear from the documents whether surveys were carried out.

Two output indicators have no evidence because they have no reported value. The safeguarding referral pathway indicator is the more consequential of the two: it is the only measure in the framework that would show whether safeguarding systems are working in practice.

**New evidence generated during the period.** None has been provided. Learning briefs would have been the programme's main evidence output, and their production is the unreported OP4.2 indicator, so it is not possible to say from this material whether any were produced. Three of four district learning meetings were held with documented action points, but the minutes have not been shared.

**Evaluation progress.** No evaluation activity is reported for the period, and none appears to have been commissioned. This is not a departure from plan — the programme design does not provide for an external evaluation in year one — but it does mean the review depends entirely on routine monitoring data.

**Data quality limitations.** Four limitations bear on how the results in this review should be read.

The reporting period offset affects every figure. All data is cut to 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025 against a contractual period of 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025.

Disaggregated data does not reconcile to headline figures in three indicators, and the caregiver breakdown is not credible on inspection.

The re-enrolment figure moved upward by 72 during a process described as removing duplicates, and the movement is unexplained.

Cost attribution at indicator level is acknowledged in the source data to be imprecise, with staff time recorded under one output that may belong under another.

None of these limitations undermines the broad picture of output delivery. Together they mean that individual figures in this review should be treated as indicative rather than audited, and that the disaggregation requirement in the award letter is not currently being met to a standard FCDO could rely on.

## Risk, Assumptions and Safeguarding

**Current risk position.** This review cannot give one. FCDO set an initial programme risk rating of Medium-High at award, reflecting delivery complexity across two districts, safeguarding sensitivity, construction-related procurement and household grant delivery. The programme design assigned output-level ratings of Medium for girls' re-entry and retention, Medium for WASH and safeguarding conditions, High for household cost barriers and Low for district evidence use. No updated ratings have been provided for the review period, and no risk register with mitigations, owners and current status exists in the material held.

The risk table below therefore reports the position at design and leaves the current column unfilled rather than inferring movement. Closing that gap is a recommendation of this review.

**Risks that materialised during the year.** Several design-stage risks can be seen in the year's delivery data even without a formal register.

Construction cost inflation materialised. WASH rehabilitation overspent by £27,900 against a forecast of £121,000, attributed to cement and transport costs, and this is the largest single financial variance in the programme.

School calendar disruption materialised. One of four district learning meetings was cancelled during the examination period, and four schools submitted attendance registers too late to be included in the reported figure.

Delivery capacity constraints materialised in a form not anticipated at design. Three schools could not be brought into the menstrual health indicator because no female focal teacher was available, and an M&E assistant post stood vacant, which both reduced spend on attendance follow-up and contributed to that indicator falling short of milestone.

**Assumptions.** The programme design does not set out an explicit assumptions register, so this review cannot report on assumptions holding or failing in a structured way. Two implicit assumptions are visible in the data. The assumption that partner schools would report on a common cycle did not hold, affecting both the attendance indicator and the reporting period question. The assumption that mobile money coverage would support grant delivery appears to have held, with 392 caregivers paid, though payment fees ran above forecast.

**Risk of funds not being used as intended.** No incident is reported. Two observations are relevant. Sixteen duplicate caregiver records were identified and removed during the year, which indicates that payment verification is operating. Against that, verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached only 68 per cent against a milestone of 75, meaning roughly a third of hardship grant households had not been verified within the intended window at the point of reporting. Follow-up verification is the main control linking payment to attendance, and its shortfall is the clearest fiduciary-adjacent weakness in the year.

**Climate and environment risk.** No climate or environmental risk assessment has been provided for the period, and the programme design does not contain one. The design identifies seasonal migration around Lake Malawi as a factor affecting the target population, and lake-shore school locations are cited as the reason Output 1 transport costs exceeded forecast, but neither is presented as a climate risk and this review does not treat them as one.

**Safeguarding.** No safeguarding update has been provided for the review period. The programme has safeguarding procedures in place by design — child safeguarding procedures, a staff code of conduct, community complaints mechanisms and referral pathways through district social welfare offices — and FCDO identified safeguarding sensitivity as a driver of the programme's Medium-High risk rating. The only indicator that would evidence whether these systems function in practice, OP2.3, is unreported.

The absence of a safeguarding update should not be read as a nil return. It is an unanswered question, and it is one FCDO is entitled to have answered.

## F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

**Financial delivery.** Expenditure attributed to indicators for the year totalled £920,420 against a forecast of £880,000, an overspend of £40,420, or 4.6 per cent above plan. Six of ten cost lines overspent and four underspent.

The largest overspend is WASH rehabilitation at £148,900 against £121,000, driven by cement and transport costs. Output 1 field delivery follows at £174,850 against £162,000, attributed to transport to lake-shore schools. Hardship grant delivery ran £5,440 over on payment fees, and learning materials £6,250 over after additional notebooks were purchased locally. Actor training exceeded forecast by £4,630 on facilitator travel.

The underspends are smaller and mostly benign. Remedial teaching came in £6,670 under forecast on lower teacher stipends. Attendance follow-up underspent by £6,020 because an M&E assistant post was vacant, which is an underspend that carries a performance cost: the same indicator fell short of its milestone. District meeting costs came in £6,300 under on lower venue costs, consistent with one meeting not taking place.

**Forecast against actual, and what is missing.** The figures above are indicator-attributed costs for the review year. They are not a programme-level expenditure statement, and the award letter requires one covering forecast against actual for the approved award. Two limitations should be understood. First, the forecast column is explicitly stated in the source data to cover the review year only, not the life of the programme, so no life-of-programme burn position can be derived from it. Second, the source data acknowledges that attribution between indicators is imperfect, with staff time recorded against attendance monitoring that may belong under Output 4. A programme-level statement against the approved £1,240,000 is outstanding.

**Value for money.** The programme's business case set a cost of approximately £987 per directly supported girl over two years, calculated on the proposal budget of £1,184,000 and a target of 1,200 girls. That budget was superseded at award: FCDO approved £1,240,000 inclusive of an agreed contingency, so the business-case unit cost no longer reflects the approved envelope and should be restated at the next review.

On economy, the design commits to local procurement for rehabilitation works and competitive pricing for learning kits. Local purchasing is visible in the year's costs, though in the case of additional notebooks it increased rather than reduced spend against forecast. Construction cost inflation, identified as a design risk, materialised and is the programme's largest variance.

On efficiency, the design proposes cost per girl re-enrolled, cost per school with completed WASH works and staff cost as a share of total spend as the measures to track. None has been calculated for this review, and the imprecision of indicator-level cost attribution would limit the reliability of the first two if they were.

On effectiveness, the intended measures are attendance, re-entry and progression results. Re-entry performance exceeded milestone; attendance fell short; progression cannot be assessed because outcome data is absent.

On equity, the intended measure is the share of support reaching girls with disabilities, girls from ultra-poor households and previously out-of-school girls. The results export carries these columns and they reconcile at column level, but because the totals aggregate across overlapping indicators they cannot be converted into a share of unique beneficiaries. An equity assessment is therefore not possible on the current data structure.

**Partner and supplier performance.** The programme budgets £214,000 for local partner delivery over two years. No partner is named in the material provided and no assessment of partner performance is available. Supplier performance is similarly unreported, though the WASH works generated verified completion certificates and school-level photographic verification, which indicates the technical supervision function is operating. The four latrine units still awaiting disposal bins are the only specific delivery shortfall identified.

**Commercial and procurement issues.** Two are visible in the cost data. Construction materials and associated transport exceeded budget by a material margin, in a programme where construction inflation was flagged as a design risk. Menstrual health supplies were procured late, contributing to that indicator falling three schools short of milestone. Neither appears to have been escalated in the material provided.

## Recommendations and Action Points

**Recommendations from this review.** Four actions are needed before the second Annual Review, and two of them determine whether that review can be completed at all.

The first is the reporting period. All AR1 data has been prepared on an October to September basis against a contractual period of 15 October to 14 October. BridgeLight should either recut results and finance data to the contractual period, or seek FCDO's written agreement to the October to September cycle as the award letter provides for. Carrying the ambiguity into a second year would compound it.

The second is outcome measurement. The programme has three outcome indicators with baselines and milestones and no mechanism currently producing results against them. The monitoring design provides for quarterly surveys; these need to be running, with a defined sample and a defined denominator, in time to report at AR2. Without this, the second Annual Review will be as unable to assess the Outcome as this one.

The third is completing the results framework. Two output indicators were not reported. Both should be reported for the period now, and the results export should carry all twelve indicators as standard.

The fourth is data quality. Disaggregated figures should reconcile to headline totals before submission, the caregiver breakdown should be corrected to reflect adult recipients, and indicators that are not person-level should not carry person-level disaggregation. Related to this, the results export should distinguish clearly between column totals and unique beneficiary counts, so that aggregate figures cannot be misread as programme reach.

Beyond these four, three further points warrant action: a current risk register with ratings, mitigations and owners; a safeguarding update for the period, including a nil return if that is the position; and a partner performance assessment covering the £214,000 local delivery budget.

**Updates on previous recommendations.** Not applicable. This is the first Annual Review of the programme and no previous review recommendations exist.

**Priorities for the next period.** Delivery priorities follow the pattern in the year's results. Sustained attendance, verified follow-up and menstrual health provision all fell short of milestone and each has a Year 2 target roughly double the Year 1 milestone, so recovery matters. The vacant M&E assistant post sits behind two of these shortfalls and filling it should be treated as a delivery action rather than an administrative one. On the evidence side, the programme's own learning function — meetings and briefs — underperformed, and it is the mechanism through which Output 4 delivers value.
